name: Illusory Superiority
description: People often rate their own abilities, traits, or judgment as better than average, even when that cannot be true for most of a group at once. Self-evaluation drifts upward when comparison targets are vague or flattering.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to skill-rating flows, creator dashboards, hiring/self-review tools, benchmark comparisons, onboarding questions, and any product that asks users to compare themselves with peers. Self-ratings often come in rosier than behavior or objective performance would justify.
prevalence_note: Well known in psychology, self-assessment, and workplace-pop-psych discussions, but the exact labels are far less common in day-to-day UX design talk than Dunning-Kruger, overconfidence, or social proof.

findings.description: A comprehensive review and meta-analysis of the better-than-average literature found a robust overall self-enhancement effect across 124 published articles, 291 independent samples, and more than 950,000 participants: people rated their abilities, attributes, and personality traits as better than the average peer (dz = 0.78, 95% CI [0.71, 0.84]). The effect was larger for personality traits than abilities, for positive rather than negative dimensions, and under several measurement/design conditions.
findings.source_title: The better-than-average effect in comparative self-evaluation: A comprehensive review and meta-analysis.
